title_content.content: Genetic Diversity and Geographic Distribution of Hantaviruses in Russia

paragraph_content.content: S. B. Garanina1 , A. E. Platonov1 , V. I. Zhuravlev1 , A. N. Murashkina2 , V. V. Yakimenko3 , A. G. Korneev4 and G. A. Shipulin1

2 Office of Federal Service ‘‘Rospotrebnadzor’’, Lipetsk, Russia

• The study concerns the most prevalent zoonotic disease in Russia and some other countries with temperate climate.
• The study starts systematic genotyping of hantaviruses in different geographic and ecological zones rather than sequencing of just few reference strains.
• Knowledge on prevalent hantavirus species and genotypes at a specific territory is critical for the development and use of adequate diagnostic tools, HFRS treatment, prognosis and control.

paragraph_content.content: Hantaviruses; haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; polymerase chain reaction; genotyping; Russia; detection methodologies
Alexander E. Platonov. Central Research Institute of Epidemiology, Novogireevskaya Str, 3a, Moscow 111123, Russia.

Haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is the most prevalent zoonotic disease in Russia. It is caused by several hantavirus species hosted by small rodents. We describe spatial and temporal patterns of HFRS incidence in the Russian Federation, and the geographic distribution of prevalent hantavirus species: Puumala (PUUV) and Dobrava (DOBV). Partial sequencing of nucleocapsid and glycoprotein genes of 117 PUUV strains and 78 DOBV strains revealed several distinct genetic subgroups. The RNA of Volga PUUV subgroup was detected in patients with HFRS and bank voles Myodes glareolus in the Volga Federal District, where the highest HFRS incidence rate has been registered yearly. The RNA of Siberian PUUV subgroup was found in M. glareolus in the trans-Ural Tyumen and Omsk Provinces, where human HFRS cases have been rare. During an HFRS outbreak in 2007 in the Central Federal District, when more than 1000 patients were affected, specific subgroups of DOBV were discovered in patients and rodents, mainly in the striped field mouse Apodemus agrarius. . The RNA of a unique DOBV subgroup was discovered in the southern semi-desert Astrakhan Province, mainly in A. agrarius and tamarisk jird Meriones tamariscinus. No human HFRS cases were diagnosed in this province. Russian PUUV and DOBV strains have no close homologues among European strains. Our DOBV strains might be genetically grouped together with Central European DOBV strains isolated from A. agrarius, but not from Apodemus flavicollis. The Volga PUUV subgroup is to some extent similar to Baltic PUUV strain, and Finnish PUUV strains resemble the strains from the Siberian PUUV subgroup. Thus, PCRbased monitoring and typing provided the opportunity to delineate and expand the area of hantaviruses in Russia and to identify their new genetic variants.

paragraph_content.content: Hantaviruses (family Bunyaviridae) are widespread in Russia, especially in the zone of deciduous woods and forest-steppe. They are causative agents of severe human zoonoses called haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Khaiboullina et al., 2005). Recently, HFRS has become the most prevalent zoonotic disease in Russia, around 5000–20 000 HFRS clinical cases are diagnosed yearly. The mean case-fatality rate is about

, and 25–50 lethal HFRS cases are registered every year. Ecological and climatic conditions vary greatly throughout the country; at least seven species of hantaviruses were found in small rodents in Russia, namely: Puumala, Dobrava, Hantaan, Seoul, Tula, Topografov and Khabarovsk (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Klein and Calisher, 2007). The first four are pathogenic to humans; the pathogenic potential of the rest is negligible or unclear (Schultze et al., 2002; Zeier et al., 2005). Most HFRS cases occur in the Volga Federal District (VOFD) (Fig. 1) and are presumably caused by Puumala virus (PUUV). This is similar to other Federal Districts except for the Far East Federal District. However, as virological and genetic typing of hantaviral clinical strains is not routine, this opinion is based on scanty fundamental research (Dekonenko and Tkachenko, 2004; Garanina et al., 2007). In southern Russia and most Siberian regions, human HFRS cases are

rarely diagnosed and animal hantaviral infection is rarely found. Therefore, the area of the hantavirus spread is breaking up in eastern Siberia, and HFRS cases in the Far East Federal District are caused by Hantaan virus and its genovariant Amur, or by Seoul virus (Yashina et al., 2000; Jiang et al., 2007). Several HFRS outbreaks in the Central Federal District were related to Dobrava virus (DOBV) (Klempa et al., 2008). PUUV is predominantly associated with the bank vole (Myodes glareolus/Clethrionomys glareolus), whereas the main host of DOBV in Russia is the striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius) (Asikainen et al., 2000; Avsic-Zupanc et al., 2000; Klempa et al., 2008).

The objective of this study consisted of PCR-based detection and genetic characterization of hantavirus strains from widely spread and different Russian regions with diverse epidemiological patterns of HFRS.

paragraph_content.content: political reasons, the original Russian names for these units may be different: for example, Bashkortostan Republic, Astrakhan Oblast and Krasnodar Krai. This difference has no epidemiological significance, so we use the generic term ‘Province’ for all these 85 units. A Province is additionally divided into several subregions (Rayons). There are usually 10–30 such subregions in each Province. This minor division will be important when we discuss the outbreak in Lipetsk Province. Data on the incidence rate of HFRS in Russian Provinces and Districts are based on the reports of Regional Centers for Sanitary and Epidemic Control summarized by the Federal Center of Hygiene and Epidemiology (http://www.fcgsen.ru).

We have studied blood plasma samples taken from 174 patients with clinically suspected HFRS. One-hundred and thirty-nine patients contracted the disease in the VOFD in 2003–2006, and 35 patients in the CEFD in 2007–2008. The samples from 112 patients

were positive in hantavirus-specific PCR. All these 112 HFRS cases were also confirmed by an indirect immunofluorescence assay. The samples from the remaining 62 patients were negative in hantavirus-specific indirect immunofluorescence assay, so other diagnoses were assigned based on clinical and/or laboratory evidence.

Rodent samples were collected in 2003–2008 in seven Russian Provinces, which differed geographically and ecologically. Rodents were trapped by officially appointed regional zoologists using either life traps or dead fall traps. The taxonomic species of the trapped rodents were determined by inspection using standard keys in accordance with the Reference Manual (Pavlinov et al., 2002). Animals were dissected in sterile conditions using disposable vessels and tools. All specimens were individually packed, labelled and stored at

Lung samples of 190 small mammals were collected in Samara Province in spring and autumn, 2003 from A. agrarius (39 samples), M. glareolus (32), common vole Microtus arvalis (75), yellow-necked mouse Apodemus flavicollis (13), common shrew Sorex araneus (11), Eurasian pygmy shrew Sorex minutus (7), harvest mouse Micromys minutus (3), least weasel Mustela nivalis (2), European water vole Arvicola terrestris (2), lesser shrew Crocidura suaveolens (2), wood mouse Apodemus sylvaticus (1), house mouse Mus musculus (1), European mole Talpa europaea (1) and steppe lemming Lagurus lagurus (1). In 2006, samples were obtained in Orenburg Province from M. glareolus (14) and wood mouse A. sylvaticus (7).

Eighteen voles M. glareolus were trapped in Tyumen Province in 2006. Six voles M. glareolus and four mice A. agrarius were trapped in Omsk Province in 2005. The samples from these 28 rodents were pre-selected from a larger collection because they were positive in hantavirus antigen specific ELISA.

A collection of 390 rodent tissue samples from Astrakhan Province was gathered in spring and autumn, 2004– 2005. It included samples of A. agrarius (180), tamarisk jird Meriones tamariscinus (136), social vole Microtus socialis (33), M. arvalis (23), M. musculus (10), S. araneus (4), piebald shrew Diplomesodon pulchellum (2), mid-day jird Meriones meridianus (1) and grey dwarf hamster Cricetulus migratorius (1).

Lung samples of 146 small mammals were collected in Lipetsk Province in the beginning of 2007, when the human HFRS outbreak occurred. There were samples from A. agrarius (61 samples), M. glareolus (26), M. arvalis (4), A. sylvaticus (33), S. araneus (12) and C. suaveolens (10). In the neighbouring Kursk Province, 24 samples from A. agrarius and two samples from M. glareolus were collected in 2007–2008.

The second screening PCR assay used the forward primer Hant M/F-ino and the reverse primer Hant M/R-ino, which are complementary to the envelope glycoprotein G2 gene sequence (Table 1). Usually, our N gene-specific PCR assay was less sensitive against Russian DOBV strains, and our G2 gene-specific PCR assay was less sensitive against Russian PUUV strains. Amplified products were sequenced using the same primers, BigDye Terminator v1.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit, and ABI Prism DNA Sequencer 3100 (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). Sequences were aligned and analysed with mega 4.0 (Tamura et al., 2007).

Since the large HFRS outbreak in 1997, the annual HFRS incidence rate in Russia has varied within the range of three to seven cases per 100 000 of population (Table 2). The regional difference was considerable (Fig. 1); the incidence rate in the VOFD (Table 2, row IV) was usually at least 10 times higher than in the other Federal Districts, and the number of cases in the VOFD averaged to nearly

of all HFRS cases in Russia. In 1997–2006, the mean annual HFRS incidence rate in the FEFD (row VII), URFD (row V) and CEFD (row I), was about 1.9, 1.5 and 1.2 cases per 100 000 of population, respectively, but a noticeable HFRS outbreak occurred in 2007 in the CEFD (row I). Among the Provinces of the SOFD (row III), human HFRS cases were only registered in the Krasnodar Province (row 6), and Volgograd Province, the latter shares a border with the VOFD. Only isolated HFRS cases were diagnosed in the SIFD (row VI). The mean HFRS case-fatality rate is the lowest in the VOFD (row IV) and the highest in the FEFD (row VII); this can be explained by the prevalence of PUUV in the former District and Hantaan virus in the latter one.

paragraph_content.content: The annual HFRS incidence rate in 13 representative Provinces is also given in Table 2; these are the Provinces where human and rodent samples were collected for our and other studies of hantaviruses. The HFRS incidence varied greatly even within Provinces belonging to the same Federal District.

In December 2006–March 2007, an HFRS outbreak took place in the part of the CEFD. Lipetsk Province was the centre of the outbreak, HFRS incidence in 2007 being 28 times higher than the historical mean for 1997–2006 (Table 2, row 2). In neighbouring Voronezh, Kursk, Belgorod, Orel, Bryansk, Tula, Ryazan and Tambov Provinces, the incidence rate increased 7.7, 4.4, 5.2, 2.6, 25, 0.7, 2.5 and 130 times, respectively. As the result, the total annual number of HFRS cases in the abovementioned Provinces reached 742 cases in comparison with 190 cases in 2006 and 112 cases in 2005.

Thirty-four PCR-positive samples were found among four species of rodents: A. agrarius (22 samples), M. musculus (1), common vole M. arvalis (4) and tamarisk jird Meriones tamariscinus (7). According to species-specific PCR, all strains belonged to Dobrava species (Table 3), which was confirmed by sequencing of 18 strains. Simultaneously with the human HFRS outbreak in 2007, the high hantavirus infection rate was found in A. agrarius, A. sylvaticus and M. glareolus trapped in Lipetsk Province (Table 3). DOBV RNA was found in mice, and PUUV RNA in voles. A similar situation was observed on rodents collected after the outbreak in Kursk Province. DOBV RNA was detected even in such atypical hosts as Sorex, Microtus and Myodes. All human HFRS cases in the Central Federal District diagnosed in this study were caused by DOBV.

Twenty-six Russian PUUV strains were characterized by sequencing of the G2 gene fragment, 275 bp (Fig. 3). This kind of typing supported the separation of Tyumen and Omsk subgroups from the Volga subgroup and the European PUUV strains.

Omsk, Astrakhan and Kursk strains still formed separate genetic branches, at the same time our Kursk strain was the most similar to Kurkino strains, isolated previously in the neighbouring Tula Province. The marker aa substitution A was found in aa position 271 of nucleocapsid protein (accession number CAA10481) in all Russian DOBV strains as opposed to G in European DOBV strains and strains from Russian Krasnodar Province (AF442622, AF442623). Only Astrakhan strains had F in position 242 and A in position 260 as opposed to L and S in all other DOBV strains. N protein sequence of Kursk and Kurkino strains had T in position 294, whereas all other strains had N.
After China, the Russian Federation is probably the country most affected by hantavirus infection. At least 5000– 7000 HFRS cases are registered every year, about
of them occurring in the European part of Russia, in comparison with nearly 2000 annual HFRS cases in the rest of

Europe (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Heyman et al., 2008). Thus, the need for HFRS investigation and control is obvious. Knowledge on prevalent hantavirus species and genotypes at specific territories is essential for the development of adequate diagnostic tools, as well as HFRS treatment and prognosis of outbreaks (Klein and Calisher, 2007). The geographic distribution of hantaviruses in Russia still needs to be further studied and described. We found only PUUV and DOBV in trans-Ural Siberian Provinces. PUUV clearly dominates in the VOFD where a HFRS incidence from 10 to 100 cases per 100 000 of population has been registered yearly. In the CEFD and NWFD of Russia, the areas of PUUV and DOBV are presumably overlapped at wide-ranging view but are most likely connected with certain landscapes and ecosystems at the local level. This connection requires additional investigation and careful monitoring. In the SOFD, hantaviruses were only found in Astrakhan Province by us (Zhuravlev et al., 2008) and in Krasnodar Province by Tkachenko’s team (Klempa et al., 2008). These findings revealed two new genetic lineages of DOBV, which have unclear epidemic potential and area of circulation. The investigation in Russian Far East and eastern Siberia explored repeatedly new genovariants and probably new

For all investigated regions, the dominant rodent host for PUUV and DOBV was M. glareolus and A. agrarius, respectively. The uncommon detection of DOBV RNA in M. glareolus, M. arvalis, M. musculus and S. araneus confirmed the possibility of interspecies infection due to close living in the same habitat (Klingstrom et al., 2002). DOBV spill-over from A. agrarius to other species might be promoted by high-rodent population densities in the CEFD, where A. agrarius and M. glareolus numbers were at least five times higher in winter 2006–2007 than in the same period in 2005–2006. It is not yet clear whether A. sylvaticus might act as a source of human DOBV infection. At least, the DOBV infection rate of these wood mice was rather high

during the outbreak in the Central Russia in 2007 (Table 3, rows 2, 4). For the first time, the hantavirus infection of jird Meriones genus in the wildlife was revealed that expanded the potential area of hantaviruses to semi-desert zones.

It was stated that PUUV is the most variable of hantaviruses (Plyusnin, 2002; Vapalahti et al., 2003). Indeed, a lot of genetic subgroups were found in both Europe and Russia (Heiske et al., 1999; Asikainen et al., 2000; Sironen et al., 2001; Dekonenko and Tkachenko, 2004; Essbauer et al., 2006; Hofmann et al., 2008; Johansson et al., 2008). It is noteworthy that in our study all partial sequences of the M and S segment were recovered by RT-PCR directly from human and rodent tissues, so they were not affected by the adaptation to the cell culture. In the highly endemic VOFD, the Volga PUUV subgroup prevailed, which seemed homogenous at the aa level but might be subdivided into more subgroups (Bashkortostan, Udmurtia, Orenburg and Samara) based on nucleotide sequence diversity of

between Bashkortostan, Udmurtia, Orenburg and Samara subgroups. This implies that these geographic subgroups are the result of spatial disconnection but not physiological adaptation. In agreement with the similarity of N and G2 protein fragments of PUUV strains, the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of

We confirmed the presence of specific PUUV genovariant in the trans-Ural Omsk Province (Dekonenko et al., 2003) and found similar strains in the neighbouring Tyumen Province. These strains carried unique aa signatures
in a hypervariable portion of nucleocapsid protein (Hughes and Friedman, 2000) instead of

, which were supposed to be characteristic for Russian (Volga) PUUV strains (Sironen et al., 2001). Thus, this subgroup might be called (western) Siberian. Human HFRS cases were very rare in these provinces. The question remains whether or not this rarity is caused by the lesser virulence of Siberian PUUV subgroup. Finnish PUUV strains resemble the strains from the Siberian PUUV subgroup but are clearly pathogenic.

The more DOBV strains are studied, the more DOBV genetic subgroups are discovered; most likely the DOBV population is as diverse as the PUUV population. We found that in Russia at least five geographic DOBV subgroups differ from each other at the nucleotide level. The possible phylogeny of Russian DOBV and PUUV subgroups looked ‘star-like’ [all lineages radiated from the single spot (Sironen et al., 2001)], therefore, no common ancestor could be identified. Russian DOBV strains had no close homologues among European strains, but might be genetically related to Central European DOBV strains isolated from A. agrarius (Klempa et al., 2005). At the aa level, there was no significant difference within strains hosted by A. agrarius, because only small genome fragments were investigated, but these strains were clearly different from strains isolated from A. flavicollis and A. ponticus (Avsic-Zupanc et al., 2000; Klempa et al., 2008). Initially Avsic-Zupanc hypothezied that A. flavicollis could have acted as the ‘donor’ and A. agrarius as the ‘recipient’ for a host-switching hantavirus. Now we see that A. agrarius-related DOBV subgroups are very diverse and widely spread in Eurasia, so their origin is less clear.

nt substitutions per site per year (Hughes and Friedman, 2000; Sironen et al., 2001; Ramsden et al., 2008). If so, DOBV subgroups found in the Lipetsk Province diverged at least

50 000 years ago, as well as PUUV strains found in the Swedish study. Even coexistence of such subgroups at the same place would be a new finding, but it seems that due to unknown reasons they are geographically separated at a small-scale level: Lipetsk–Usman strains have not yet been found in the Lipetsk–Dobrinka subregion and vice versa (Fig. 4).

Our findings confirmed the necessity to discriminate the clinical HFRS disease caused by classical Dobrava– Belgrade strains and Dobrava strains hosted by A. agrarius (Vapalahti et al., 2003; Golovljova et al., 2007). During the HFRS outbreak in the CEFD in the winter of 2006– 2007, all available clinical strains were genotyped as a Dobrava-Aa genovariant (Table 3, Fig. 4). The disease was generally mild or moderate, the case-fatality rate was about
. The same was true for the HFRS outbreak in the Lipetsk Province in the winter of 2001–2002 (Klempa et al., 2008).

The reliability of diagnostics by PCR depends on genetic variability for the detection of viral nucleic acids in unknown samples. The results of this study have already been implemented in the development of RT-PCR assays manufactured by the Central Institute of Epidemiology, Moscow, and used for hantavirus RNA detection in Russia. Using this RT-PCR assay and human plasma samples taken at the first 4 days of disease, we were able to diagnose

of HFRS cases confirmed serologically (Garanina et al., 2007). The analysis of genetic diversity and geographic distribution of hantaviruses in Eurasia may in the future contribute to better diagnostics and treatment, as well as to a more complete understanding of the factors that determine hantavirus pathogenesis and ability to cause human epidemics.
